Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> Banking and Finance | Economy | National MPC cuts policy rate to 11% from 14 percent Source : James Eshun 18 November 2026 2:46pm Dr. Johnson Asiama ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) of the Bank of Ghana (BoG) has cut its Monetary Policy Rate by 300 basis points to 11 per cent, as improving economic conditions and declining market interest rates provide room for further easing of monetary policy.
The reduction from 14 per cent was announced by Governor of the Bank of Ghana, Dr Johnson Asiama, following the 133rd Monetary Policy Committee meeting held from November 16 to 18, 2026.
The decision comes amid sustained improvements in domestic economic activity, easing credit conditions and expectations that inflation will gradually return to the central bank's medium-term target.
Dr Asiama said the committee had observed significant improvements in the economy, with growth remaining firm and supported by an expansion in private sector credit.
“Taken together, the Committee noted significant improvements in domestic macroeconomic conditions. Domestic growth has remained firm, supported by easing credit conditions and expansion of private sector credit, and is expected to continue for the remainder of the year,” he said.
The Governor explained that prevailing market interest rates had fallen below the existing policy rate of 14 per cent, indicating that the effective monetary policy stance was already lower than the announced rate.
He said recent reforms to the Bank's monetary operations framework had strengthened liquidity management and improved the transmission of monetary policy signals to money market rates.
“Recent reforms to the Bank's monetary operations framework have strengthened liquidity management and improved the transmission of monetary policy signals to money market rates,” Dr Asiama said.
The committee has consequently introduced additional reforms to the monetary operations framework, including replacing the current open market operations instrument with a seven-day instrument and narrowing the monetary policy corridor from plus or minus 400 basis points to plus or minus 100 basis points around the policy rate.
The reduction in the policy rate is expected to further ease borrowing costs and support businesses and households as credit conditions improve.
Growth in private sector credit increased to 37.2 per cent in October 2026 from 13.9 per cent a year earlier, while real private sector credit growth rose to 30 per cent from 5.4 per cent over the same period.
Banks' average lending rates also declined to 15.8 per cent in October from 22.2 per cent in October 2025.
Headline inflation, however, increased marginally to 5.5 per cent in October from 5.2 per cent in September, although it remained below the lower bound of the Bank's medium-term target.
The Bank said inflation was expected to gradually move back into the target range over the medium term, but identified risks including crude oil price shocks, the impact of El Niño on food production and quarterly adjustments in utility tariffs.
On the external front, gross international reserves stood at US$12.1 billion as of November 17, 2026, equivalent to 4.4 months of import cover, down from US$13.8 billion at the end of December 2025.
The next Monetary Policy Committee meeting is scheduled for January 2027.
